hero.title: Obsidian
hero.signatureLine: Natural volcanic glass. A history of fire held still.
hero.condensedIntro: Obsidian forms when silica-rich lava cools before a crystal structure can develop. Its familiar black glass can carry iron-rich color, pale snowflakes, metallic sheen, or bands of hidden rainbow, each preserving a different part of the lava’s story.

meetObsidianFamily.title: Meet the Obsidian Family
meetObsidianFamily.intro: Obsidian may begin as dark volcanic glass, but bubbles, mineral-rich patches, crystals, and hidden layers can transform how each variety looks and reflects light.

members.name: Black Obsidian
members.identSentence: The clearest expression of Obsidian’s dark volcanic glass.

members.name: Gold Sheen Obsidian
members.identSentence: Fine internal features return the light as a warm golden glow.
members.chosenFor: Personal power, direction, and recognizing what supports forward movement.

members.name: Silver Sheen Obsidian
members.identSentence: Reflective internal layers create a cool silver glow across the dark surface.
members.chosenFor: Clarity, reflection, and seeing beneath appearances.

members.name: Rainbow Obsidian
members.identSentence: Hidden bands reveal changing colors when the stone turns in the light.
members.chosenFor: Emotional healing, hope, and approaching difficult truths with greater softness.

members.name: Snowflake Obsidian
members.identSentence: Pale radiating crystals mark places where part of the volcanic glass began to change.
members.chosenFor: Balance, grounded perspective, and recognizing patterns.

members.name: Mahogany Obsidian
members.identSentence: Iron-rich reddish-brown areas interrupt the black glass with earthy color.
members.chosenFor: Steady grounding, strength, and gentler emotional work.

howLavaBecomesObsidian.title: How Lava Becomes Obsidian
howLavaBecomesObsidian.intro: Obsidian begins as silica-rich lava. When the lava cools very quickly, its ingredients are held in place before they can arrange into a repeating crystal structure. The result is natural volcanic glass.
howLavaBecomesObsidian.closing: Its glassy structure gives Obsidian its smooth polish, curved fracture, and ability to preserve bubbles, layers, and patterns from the moving lava.

lavaPreserves.title: What the Lava Preserves
lavaPreserves.intro: Before it hardened, Obsidian was moving lava. Bubbles, iron-rich patches, and very thin layers were stretched and held in place as the glass cooled. Those traces became the patterns collectors recognize today.

headers: WHAT WAS HELD IN THE GLASS
rows: Small crystals forming in the glass

colorInGlass.title: Color in the Glass, Color in the Light
colorInGlass.intro: Some Obsidian carries color in the glass itself. Other pieces look dark until light catches hidden layers inside.

cards.title: Color in the Glass
cards.body: Mahogany Obsidian’s earthy red-brown areas belong to the glass itself.

cards.title: Color in the Light
cards.body: Rainbow Obsidian’s hidden bands appear when the stone turns in the light.

namesToVerify.title: Names to Verify
paragraphs: Bright, evenly colored pink, yellow, aqua, blue, or purple pieces sold as Obsidian are often manufactured glass. Natural Obsidian can flash some of these colors in reflected light, but that is not the same as having a uniformly colored body.

Manufactured glass can still hold metaphysical meaning. In modern practice, yellow versions are commonly chosen for confidence, joy, and Solar Plexus work, while pink versions are associated with love, compassion, and heart-centered healing. These associations come primarily from color and intention rather than a verified natural Obsidian identity.

photo.alt: Material sold under the market name Yellow Obsidian

collection.title: Obsidian in Your Collection
collection.intro: Obsidian rewards looking beyond black. The right piece depends on whether you want the family’s most direct grounding presence, a steadier patterned form, or reflective color that only appears when the stone moves.

cards.title: Choose the Strength
paragraphs: Black Obsidian offers the family’s most direct grounding and protective presence. Mahogany and Snowflake Obsidian can feel steadier and gentler, while Rainbow Obsidian brings a more heart-centered form of emotional perspective.

cards.title: Turn the Stone
paragraphs: Gold Sheen, Silver Sheen, and Rainbow Obsidian reveal themselves through changing light. Turn the piece slowly rather than judging it from a single angle.

cards.title: Protect the Polish
paragraphs: Obsidian is glass. Protect polished pieces from knocks and harder stones, and clean them gently to preserve their surface.

obsidian.closingCallout: Obsidian reminds us that what looks still and dark may carry a history of fire, movement, and hidden light.

hero.title: Copper Minerals Family Guide
hero.signatureLine: Copper paints in blue and green.
hero.condensedIntro: Copper does not create just one recognizable mineral. As water and oxygen move through copper-bearing rock, they can transform the material near the surface and produce vivid new minerals in cracks, pockets, and open spaces.

oneDeposit.title: One Deposit, Many Outcomes
paragraphs: Native copper can occur in metallic form, often branching, twisting, or spreading in thin sheets. It is also the element behind the vivid blues and greens of azurite, malachite, chrysocolla, and many other minerals in this guide.

Near the surface of a copper deposit, copper combines with oxygen, carbon, sulfur, silica, and water. As conditions change, different mineral species can form—sometimes side by side within the same deposit.

rows: Red, emerald green, or compact blue-green
Minerals overlap or replace one another

meetCopperFamily.title: Featured Copper Minerals
meetCopperFamily.intro: These six minerals offer a clear introduction to the copper family, showing the vivid color, varied forms, and close mineral relationships that make it so distinctive.

members.name: Azurite
paragraphs: Azurite is known for its intense blue, ranging from rich royal blue to nearly black. It may form as distinct crystals, rounded growths, velvety coatings, or massive material.
Often found with malachite, some azurite gradually alters into malachite over time.

members.name: Malachite
paragraphs: Malachite ranges from bright green to nearly black-green, often forming bands, rings, ripples, or rounded growth patterns.
In polished pieces, those patterns reveal layers of mineral growth—not painted or added color.

members.name: Chrysocolla
paragraphs: Chrysocolla ranges from pale blue to vivid turquoise-green. It often appears as coatings, uneven patches, or massive material mixed with quartz, malachite, and other copper minerals.
Because its appearance varies widely, color alone is rarely enough to identify it.

members.name: Shattuckite
paragraphs: Shattuckite is usually blue to blue-green and may form in fibrous, radiating, or velvety growths. In mixed specimens, it can resemble chrysocolla or azurite.
The rarer copper mineral plancheite can look similar, particularly when it forms pale blue fibrous growths.

members.name: Dioptase
paragraphs: Dioptase forms brilliant green crystals with a glassy surface. Its color may resemble emerald, but dioptase is much softer and belongs to an entirely different mineral group.
Even small crystals can appear unusually vivid because of the mineral's strong green color and clarity.

members.name: Cuprite
paragraphs: Cuprite introduces a surprising color into the copper family. It may appear deep red, brown-red, or nearly black, sometimes with a metallic or reflective surface.
When cuprite grows with blue-green copper minerals, the contrast can be dramatic.

otherCopperMinerals.title: More Expressions of Copper
otherCopperMinerals.intro: Copper's reach extends beyond the six minerals above. Turquoise, ajoite, and plancheite each have their own identity within the wider copper-mineral story.

paragraphs: Turquoise is a blue to green copper-bearing mineral that often forms in veins or nodules. Its matrix, treatments, and long history as a gemstone give it a visual identity of its own.
Ajoite is much rarer. It is usually encountered as blue-green inclusions or delicate growths, often associated with quartz and other copper minerals.

members.name: Plancheite
members.alt: Plancheite specimen with pale blue fibrous growth, Shangulowé Mine, Katanga, Democratic Republic of the Congo
paragraphs: Plancheite is a rare blue copper silicate that commonly forms fibrous or radiating growths. Its pale blue color and texture can make it resemble Shattuckite, especially in mixed specimens.

colorComparison.title: Blue, Green, or Both?
paragraphs: Color offers a useful starting point, but it cannot confirm a mineral's identity.
Azurite is usually blue. Malachite and dioptase are usually green. Chrysocolla, shattuckite, turquoise, and ajoite may fall somewhere between the two.

Texture often gives the next clue. Distinct glassy crystals suggest something different from a soft-looking coating, a fibrous growth, or a polished banded surface. The surrounding matrix and associated minerals also matter.
colorComparison.pullQuote: A blue-green color can narrow the possibilities, but it cannot identify the stone by itself.

growTogether.title: When Copper Minerals Grow Together
growTogether.intro: Copper minerals frequently share the same fractures and pockets. They may grow side by side, overlap, or become so closely intergrown that separating them by sight is difficult.

features.title: Azurmalachite
features.alt: Azurmalachite specimen showing both blue azurite and green malachite
features.body: Azurmalachite contains both azurite and malachite. Its blues and greens may remain distinct or merge into flowing patterns.

features.title: Chrysocolla in Quartz and Gem Silica
features.alt: Quartz, chrysocolla, and chalcedony (gem silica) association from the Globe-Miami District, Arizona
features.body: Quartz can make chrysocolla-rich material harder and more durable. Gem silica is the rarer, more specific form: translucent chalcedony colored blue or green by copper.

features.title: Sonora Sunrise
features.alt: Representative cuprite, tenorite, and chrysocolla association from the Milpillas Mine, Sonora, Mexico
features.body: Sonora Sunrise, also called Sonora Sunset, combines blue-green chrysocolla with red cuprite in a dark matrix.

features.title: Mixed Copper Minerals and Quantum Quattro
features.alt: Malachite and chrysocolla from the Katanga Copper Crescent
features.body: Quantum Quattro is a trade name for mixed blue-green copper minerals with quartz. Its reported ingredients vary, so the name does not represent one fixed composition.

copperCare.title: Copper Minerals in Your Collection
copperCare.intro: Copper minerals bring vivid color and unmistakable presence to a collection. Thoughtful display, gentle handling, and a little attention to their natural sensitivities help that character remain at its best.

panels.title: Handle Gently
panels.body: Many copper minerals are softer, more porous, or more brittle than they appear. Avoid soaking them, scrubbing delicate surfaces, or using chemical cleaners unless the mineral has been positively identified and the cleaning method is known to be safe.

panels.title: Avoid Dust, Drinking Water, and Elixirs
panels.body: Do not grind, sand, drill, or polish copper minerals without appropriate equipment and dust controls. Keep them out of drinking water and crystal elixirs, and wash your hands after handling rough or dusty specimens.

closingEssay.title: A Family Written in Color
paragraphs: Copper minerals show how much can happen inside one small pocket of rock. Blue becomes green. One mineral coats another. Clear boundaries soften into mixtures.
The closer you look, the less chaotic the color becomes. What first appears to be a wild blue-green stone begins to reveal a record of water, chemistry, and change.
closingEssay.finalLine: In copper minerals, change does not disappear. It becomes color.

hero.title: Beryl Family Guide
hero.imageAlt: Five numbered Beryl variety specimens: Golden Beryl, Heliodor, Emerald, Aquamarine, and Morganite
hero.imageLegend: 1 Golden Beryl · 2 Heliodor · 3 Emerald · 4 Aquamarine · 5 Morganite
hero.condensedIntro: Beryl is the family hiding in plain sight. The ocean blue of Aquamarine, the lush green of Emerald, the blush of Morganite, and the glow of Heliodor all begin with the same crystal. Change only a few trace ingredients, and one mineral becomes an entire color story.

whatBerylIs.title: What Beryl Is
paragraphs: Emerald feels like its own world. So does Aquamarine. But beneath their dramatically different colors, both share Beryl's clear, six-sided architecture.

Morganite brings pink and peach. Heliodor brings yellow and gold. Goshenite reveals the family with the color turned off. Each is Beryl, shaped by the small amounts of other elements present while the crystal was growing.

meetBerylFamily.title: Meet Five Beryl Expressions
meetBerylFamily.intro: The five Beryl varieties in the Still Point Lapidary catalog share one mineral identity but offer distinctly different colors, appearances, and energetic traditions.

members.name: Emerald
members.identSentence: Emerald ranges from vivid green to bluish green. Natural inclusions may give it a mossy or garden-like interior.

members.name: Aquamarine
members.identSentence: Aquamarine ranges from pale blue to blue-green and is often transparent with a clear, glassy appearance.
members.chosenFor: Calm communication, courage, and emotional steadiness

members.name: Morganite
members.identSentence: Morganite ranges from pale pink to peach, usually with a soft, luminous clarity.

members.name: Heliodor
members.identSentence: Heliodor ranges from pale yellow to rich golden yellow and may carry a subtle greenish tone.

members.name: Goshenite
members.identSentence: Goshenite is colorless Beryl. It may be transparent and glassy or softly clouded by natural inclusions.

builtInSixSides.title: Built in Six Sides
builtInSixSides.imageAlt: Beryl crystal on Muscovite matrix showing a six-sided columnar form
paragraphs: Beryl belongs to the hexagonal crystal system and commonly grows as a six-sided column. Crystals may be short and broad or long and slender, with flat sides running along their length.
The six-sided outline is especially clear when the crystal's end remains intact. Some crystals finish with a broad, flat top, while others are broken or partly embedded in surrounding rock.

This shape can help connect specimens that otherwise appear unrelated. A green Emerald crystal and a blue Aquamarine crystal may share the same columnar form even though their colors are completely different.
Beryl may also grow much larger than many collectors expect. When a crystal has enough room and time to develop, it can form substantial columns with clearly defined faces.

berylColor.title: How Beryl Gets Its Color
berylColor.intro: Pure Beryl is colorless. Its varieties appear when very small amounts of other elements become part of the crystal as it grows.
paragraphs: Aquamarine and Heliodor offer one of the family's most interesting comparisons. Iron contributes to both varieties, but differences within the crystal determine whether the result appears blue or yellow.
Color can also vary within a single crystal. A specimen may be darker at one end, paler through the center, or divided into visible zones that record changes during growth.

berylNaming.title: Understanding Beryl Names
berylNaming.intro: Most Beryl variety names describe color, but some boundaries are less exact than others.

cards.label: Emerald and Green Beryl
cards.body: Emerald is the name used for strongly colored green to bluish-green Beryl. Lighter or less saturated material may be sold simply as Green Beryl. Experts do not always agree on the precise point where Green Beryl becomes Emerald.

cards.label: Heliodor and Golden Beryl
cards.body: Heliodor, Golden Beryl, and Yellow Beryl are used for the family's yellow range. The names often overlap, although some sellers reserve Heliodor for stronger golden or slightly greenish material.

cards.label: Goshenite
cards.body: Goshenite is the accepted variety name for colorless Beryl. It may also be described plainly as Colorless Beryl.

cards.label: Red Beryl
cards.body: Red Beryl is a genuine but exceptionally rare Beryl variety colored by manganese. It belongs in the family lesson, but it is not part of the fixed Still Point Lapidary catalog. It receives no Stone ID, Quick View link, or catalog badge.

collection.title: Beryl in Your Collection
collection.intro: Beryl is durable, but crystal edges and natural fractures can still chip. Emerald needs extra care because inclusions and clarity treatments may make it more vulnerable than other members of the family.

careForIt.intro: Beryl resists ordinary scratching but can still chip or fracture.
bullets: Dust gently with a clean, soft cloth or very soft brush.
When appropriate, use lukewarm water and mild soap, then dry thoroughly.
Avoid harsh cleaners, sudden temperature changes, and prolonged soaking.
Never steam or ultrasonically clean Emeralds or pieces with unknown treatments.

collection.rememberThis: Beryl ranks 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale, but hardness is not toughness. It resists scratches; it does not resist every impact. Crystal points, thin edges, and existing fractures remain vulnerable.
collection.watchFor: Many Emeralds are clarity enhanced with oil or resin inside surface-reaching fractures. Heat, chemicals, steam, and ultrasonic cleaning can damage the filling or the stone. Ask about treatments before cleaning valuable Beryl.

beryl.closingCallout: Beryl shows how one enduring structure can make room for many distinct expressions.
